facts.claim: "False Idols" was released June 30, 2023 by XO / Republic Records on the two-track single The Idol Episode 5 Part 1 (Music from the HBO Original Series).
The writing credits are Abel Tesfaye (The Weeknd), Mike Dean, Suzanna Son, Dominique Jones (Lil Baby) and Jordan Holt-May.
Mike Dean is credited as producer, mixer and mastering engineer, with The Weeknd also credited as producer.
The Weeknd previewed the song on an Instagram live session on June 27, 2023, with producer Mike Dean in the studio.
The song is the second collaboration between The Weeknd and Lil Baby. Their first was "Hurricane" on Kanye West's 2021 album Donda.
Suzanna Son, an actress in The Idol, sings the hook. American Songwriter notes that the lyrics include double entendres about cocaine and Chrome Hearts.

The song appears in The Idol Season 1, Episode 5 ("Jocelyn Forever"), where Suzanna Son's character Chloe performs it for Finklestein, Chaim and Nikki as they wait for Joss to arrive. Tunefind also lists it in Episode 4, where Chloe plays and sings it in the studio.
It was released the same day as the solo Weeknd track "Like a God", ahead of the series finale. Complex reports that both tracks include co-production from Mike Dean.
The Idol soundtrack material was released as per-episode EPs. It was originally planned as a single soundtrack album, The Idol, Vol. 1, which was scrapped.

Tesfaye has said Hurry Up Tomorrow is probably his last hurrah as the Weeknd. He has said he still wants to kill the Weeknd persona, and he partly attributes losing his voice on tour to exhaustion from juggling the After Hours til Dawn Tour with The Idol.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Weeknd's alternative R&B and pop soundtrack work, written for HBO's The Idol and built around Mike Dean's synth-heavy production plus a trap-leaning Lil Baby guest verse.

draft:
The prayer at the center of **False Idols** is sung so sweetly that its meaning nearly slips past: "Makes you hurt again / So you can heal and say amen." That is a description of abuse dressed as worship, a god who wounds you so the comfort feels earned. Suzanna Son sings the hook, and the song lives in the space between that hymn and the rap around it, where people with every reason to feel secure keep admitting they don't.

The verses are a ledger. Contracts with "baseball numbers," eight-figure taxes, a million for an hour-long set, diamonds that "really be diamonds." The bragging is real, but it keeps snagging on something. "But I went through a lot for this money and fame" turns the flex into a receipt for damage. Then the narrator mentions a big brother at the end of his habeas appeals: "I talk to him daily, I told him he still comin' home." The next line worries the brother will hear it as empty talk. Pride and guilt sit in the same bar, and neither wins. Later the paradise boasts collapse into "But these false idols got me terrified," repeated until it stops sounding like a pose.

The production keeps all this cool on the surface. A low synth pad hangs under everything, fast hi-hats tick steadily, and the kick and snare land crisp and punchy. The groove is laid-back and mid-tempo, unhurried even when the words are frightened. The rap is mixed dry and close, clear with a slightly nasal edge, confident and conversational, with no harmonies padding it out. That intimacy matters. The fear arrives at speaking volume, as if nobody's supposed to overhear.

Abel Tesfaye wrote it with Mike Dean, Son, Dominique Jones (Lil Baby) and Jordan Holt-May. Dean produced, mixed and mastered it, with The Weeknd co-producing. It's the second time The Weeknd and Lil Baby have worked together, after "Hurricane" on Kanye West's *Donda*. It was written for HBO's *The Idol*. In episode five, Son's character Chloe performs it for a room of handlers waiting on the show's star, Joss. Heard that way, the closing chant "He will find her / He will fix her" stops being devotional and starts sounding like a threat. Lines like "We still walkin' with the cameras off" and "She ain't actin', I'm not an actor" blur the show into the song. The track came out the same day as The Weeknd's solo "Like a God," and its outro trails off on that same phrase.

The song makes you hear wealth as a wall around fear, and its prettiest melody is the one asking you to thank whoever hurt you.
